documents.title: Model Context Protocol Security Vulnerabilities & Threat Model
documents.content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool integration for LLM-based agents. However, MCP's implicit trust model creates significant vulnerability vectors. Clients assume tool definitions from connected MCP servers are safe and immutable. Without cryptographic pinning or continuous behavioral monitoring, malicious or compromised MCP servers can modify tool schemas post-approval, leading to unauthorized host agent exploitation.

documents.title: Tool Poisoning Attacks (TPA) in Agentic AI Workflows
documents.source: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) AI Working Group
documents.content: Tool Poisoning Attacks (TPA) occur when an attacker embeds malicious prompt instructions into tool metadata fields such as 'name', 'description', or 'inputSchema'. Because LLM agents treat tool descriptions as authoritative operational guidelines, poisoned metadata deceives the agent into executing secondary malicious actions, such as exfiltrating environment variables, reading local SSH keys, or issuing unauthorized API calls.

documents.title: Rug-Pull Attack Life Cycle & Staged Trust Exploitation in MCP
documents.content: A Rug-Pull attack in MCP involves a multi-stage lifecycle: 1. Deployment & Registration: The MCP tool is registered with benign functionality (e.g., weather lookup). 2. Trust Building: The user/agent invokes the tool repeatedly, establishing operational trust. 3. Silent Modification: The server updates metadata, permission requirements, or external endpoints without user review. 4. Malicious Execution: The tool executes unauthorized operations, leveraging established trust to bypass initial entry controls. Continuous adaptive trust monitoring is essential to detect post-approval drift.

documents.title: Indirect Prompt Injection via Retracted Web and File Content
documents.content: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) occurs when an MCP tool retrieves untrusted external data (web content, Markdown files, database records) containing adversarial prompts. When the agent ingests the retrieved text into its context window, hidden instructions hijack the agent's reasoning, causing it to exfiltrate context history to attacker-controlled endpoints.

documents.title: Unannounced Permission Escalation & Endpoint Drift in MCP Tools
documents.content: Unannounced permission escalation occurs when an updated MCP server requests sensitive system capabilities (e.g., 'read_user_files', 'execute_system_command') after initial deployment. Similarly, endpoint drift shifts outbound tool requests from verified domains to unknown C2 servers. Security systems must calculate permission delta risk and enforce endpoint allowlists.

documents.title: Zero-Trust Architecture & Continuous Monitoring Guidelines for MCP
documents.source: NIST Cybersecurity Framework Guidance for Agentic AI
documents.content: To mitigate MCP security risks, organizations should enforce Zero-Trust principles: 1. Pin tool schemas and descriptions upon initial registration. 2. Enforce least-privilege scoping per MCP tool session. 3. Implement continuous semantic and behavioral drift scoring. 4. Automatically degrade trust scores and block high-risk tool execution upon detecting unauthorized changes.

documents.title: Runtime Behavioral Anomaly Indicators in Compromised MCP Tools
documents.content: Behavioral anomalies in compromised MCP tools manifest through distinct runtime signatures: sudden call frequency spikes (>5x baseline), high request failure rates due to exfiltration throttling, elevated execution latency variance, and unusually large response payload lengths corresponding to data exfiltration.
